title: The Central Bank Balance-Sheet Trilemma
summary: Federal Reserve economists Duygan-Bump and Kahn present a 'balance sheet trilemma' framework explaining why central banks can achieve only two of three goals simultaneously: a small balance sheet, low volatility of short-term rates, and limited market intervention. The Fed's balance sheet grew from approximately $800 billion (6% of GDP) in December 2005 to roughly $6.5 trillion (21% of GDP) in December 2025, with the balance-sheet reduction process concluding on December 1, 2025. The authors demonstrate that as reserves fall relative to outstanding Treasuries, money-market rate sensitivity to liquidity shocks increases, explaining why shrinking the balance sheet forces a tradeoff between higher rate volatility or more frequent central bank market operations.
key_points: Fed balance sheet expanded from ~$800 billion (6% of GDP, Dec 2005) to ~$6.5 trillion (21% of GDP, Dec 2025), primarily via QE after GFC and during COVID-19 pandemic
In 2019, FOMC shifted to an ample-reserves regime from the prior scarce-reserves framework for targeting short-term interest rates
Balance-sheet reduction concluded December 1, 2025; Fed announced reserve management purchases on December 10, 2025 to maintain ample reserves
The 'balance sheet trilemma': central banks can achieve only two of three goals—small balance sheet, low short-term rate volatility, or limited market intervention
Repo rate sensitivity (Tri-Party General Collateral Rate spread over ON RRP) to Treasury General Account changes increases as reserves decline relative to outstanding Treasuries
When reserve buffers are thin, even small liquidity shocks translate into outsized increases in short-term funding rates across markets
Quarter-end balance-sheet effects, Treasury issuance, and foreign repo pool movements cause predictable increases in rate sensitivity when reserves are scarce
why_it_matters: This research directly informs the ongoing debate about the appropriate steady-state size of the Fed's balance sheet post-QT. Market participants, policymakers, and researchers need to understand that choosing a smaller balance sheet has concrete operational costs: either accepting higher money-market rate volatility or tolerating more frequent central bank market interventions. The trilemma framework clarifies these tradeoffs for anyone watching reserve adequacy, repo market functioning, or the Fed's future balance-sheet trajectory.
market_structure_context: The source provides detailed market structure analysis of money-market mechanics. Key findings: (1) As reserves fall relative to outstanding Treasuries, the spread of the Tri-Party General Collateral Rate (TGCR) over the ON RRP rate becomes more responsive to changes in the Treasury General Account (TGA); (2) Similar sensitivity increases occur with Treasury issuance, quarter-end effects, and foreign repo pool balances; (3) Money-market volatility (90-day rolling standard deviation of the TGCR-ON RRP spread) rises as reserves become scarcer; (4) The Fed's standing facilities (Standing Repo operations, Overnight Reverse Repo operations, Discount Window) serve as passive tools to allow reserves to respond to market demand without active open market operations. Authors reference Gissler et al. (2025), Cordes et al. (2025), Bostrom et al. (2025), and Alquist et al. (2022) for empirical support.
